title: The lost art of memory
gist: A short culture notebook: Paul Lay uses Frances Yates' 1966 'The Art of Memory' to argue that rising literacy and printing eroded human memorisation capacity even as it boosted reading, then recommends a new Sibelius symphony cycle and reflects on the TV adaptation of Ford Madox Ford's 'Parade's End'.

insights.claim: The rise of printing and mass literacy had a documented negative side effect: it substantially eroded human capacity for memorisation, since oral cultures (e.g. Homeric bards reciting roughly 30,000 lines of verse) trained a 'muscular memory' through repeated practice that became less necessary, and thus less developed, once texts could be written down.
insights.speaker: Paul Lay
insights.so_what: A historical precedent directly relevant to current debates about AI/digital tools further eroding cognitive skills (memory, concentration) — literacy itself already set this precedent centuries before printing.

insights.claim: Frances A. Yates' 1966 book 'The Art of Memory' remains, in the author's view, the best study of mnemonic technique, tracing the subject from Simonides of Ceos (5th-century BC Athenian poet) through to Giordano Bruno in the early age of print.
insights.speaker: Paul Lay
insights.so_what: A specific reference work for anyone researching the history and mechanics of mnemonic systems, relevant to renewed interest in memory techniques amid concerns about digital cognitive decline.

insights.claim: Conductor Jukka-Pekka Saraste's new recording of Jean Sibelius' seven symphonies with the Helsinki Philharmonic Orchestra is praised as his third and best cycle, distinguished by a 'cool', undemonstrative, icily composed style, particularly in the Fourth and Sixth symphonies.
insights.speaker: Paul Lay
insights.so_what: A specific new classical-music release recommendation for readers/investors tracking cultural output or classical-recording market activity.

insights.claim: Tom Stoppard's TV adaptation of Ford Madox Ford's 'Parade's End' quartet, starring Benedict Cumberbatch, omits the final novel ('Last Post') from its otherwise highly acclaimed five-part series.
insights.speaker: Paul Lay
insights.so_what: Notes a specific adaptation choice (dropping the final novel) relevant to anyone assessing the completeness/fidelity of the TV version versus the source quartet.
